correctness.rationale: Every function on the union of two distinct lines has a unique decomposition as h1 on the first line plus h2 with h2(0)=0 on the second. The two complete sets of Fourier-zero equations are equivalent to (1), using all points of the union. The Gram determinant equals det[u,v]^2 and is nonzero. If any of A,B,C vanishes, invertibility follows by the forced-constant Fourier-transform argument and h2(0)=0. Otherwise the pair of equations reduces bijectively to H2(rho z)=H2(z), with H2(0) fixed by the one sum-zero constraint. Exactly (q−1)/ord(rho) independent orbit scalars survive. This proof does not depend on finite tests. The included exact modular checker verifies all 436 pairs for ten fields as corroboration, with modular-vs-complex limitations explicit.

value.rationale: Principal Fourier sampling on a union of two linear subspaces is a canonical finite-harmonic interpolation problem: injectivity and kernel dimension are natural exact invariants. The sharp and nontrivial dichotomy is that every nonisotropic nonorthogonal line pair fails self-sampling, while all degenerate-pairing cases are invertible. The entire defect varies arithmetically through multiplicative order, yielding a complete classification for infinitely many prime powers rather than a narrow computed slice. The orbit proof identifies all missing interpolation directions and informs construction of sampling sets.
